body:
The beginnings of Indian literary traditions

Ancient Indian literature developed through several religious, philosophical and linguistic traditions. Its earliest surviving extensive literary corpus is Vedic literature, composed in Vedic Sanskrit. Much of this literature was preserved orally for centuries before being recorded in manuscripts.

Teachers transmitted hymns to pupils through carefully regulated recitation. This oral tradition preserved not only the words but also their pronunciation and accent. Consequently, the date of a surviving manuscript may be much later than the date when its contents were originally composed.

The 4 Vedas

The word Veda means knowledge. Each Veda contains a collection of sacred compositions known as a Samhita. The Rigveda is the oldest of the 4 Vedas, with its principal period of composition generally placed around 1500–1000 BCE.

VedaPrincipal contentsAssociated feature
RigvedaHymns praising deities and exploring philosophical questionsEarliest Vedic collection
SamavedaVerses arranged for melodic chantingClosely connected with Indian musical traditions
YajurvedaSacrificial formulas and instructionsPerformance of Vedic sacrifices
AtharvavedaPrayers, protective charms, healing and philosophical compositionsDomestic life, health and everyday concerns

The Rigveda consists of 10 Mandalas containing 1028 hymns, known as Suktas, in its commonly preserved Shakala recension. Mandalas 2–7 are generally regarded as its oldest core and are associated with particular families of seers.

Important Rigvedic deities include Indra, associated with strength and warfare; Agni, associated with fire and sacrifice; Varuna, associated with cosmic and moral order; and Soma, associated with a sacred ritual drink and its divine personification.

The Purusha Sukta describes the origin of the social order through the cosmic being Purusha. The Nasadiya Sukta raises philosophical questions about the origin of the universe. Both occur in the 10th Mandala of the Rigveda.

The Samaveda borrows much of its verbal material from the Rigveda, but arranges it for chanting. The Yajurveda is preserved in 2 principal traditions: Shukla Yajurveda and Krishna Yajurveda. The Shukla tradition generally separates sacrificial formulas from explanatory material, whereas the Krishna tradition combines them more closely.

The 4 principal divisions of Vedic literature

Vedic literature is broader than the Samhitas. Its associated texts explain ritual, explore its symbolic meaning and investigate philosophical questions.

  • Samhitas: Collections of hymns, prayers, chants and sacrificial formulas.
  • Brahmanas: Mainly prose explanations of sacrifices, rituals and their significance. The Aitareya Brahmana is associated with the Rigveda, while the Shatapatha Brahmana belongs to the Shukla Yajurveda.
  • Aranyakas: Texts concerned with the deeper and symbolic meaning of rituals, traditionally associated with forest contemplation.
  • Upanishads: Philosophical texts examining ultimate reality, the self, knowledge, existence and liberation.

The Upanishads include philosophical discussions about Atman, the individual self, and Brahman, the ultimate reality. Important early examples are the Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya Upanishads. The term Vedanta, meaning the conclusion of the Veda, is closely associated with Upanishadic thought.

Shruti, Smriti and the Vedangas

Shruti, meaning that which is heard, refers to the Vedic corpus regarded as revealed knowledge. Smriti, meaning that which is remembered, refers to traditionally transmitted compositions such as the epics, Puranas and Dharma texts.

The 6 Vedangas are auxiliary disciplines developed to support the correct understanding and preservation of the Vedas:

  • Shiksha: Phonetics and pronunciation.
  • Kalpa: Ritual procedures.
  • Vyakarana: Grammar.
  • Nirukta: Etymology and explanation of difficult words.
  • Chandas: Poetic metre.
  • Jyotisha: Astronomical calculations, particularly those connected with ritual timing.

Historical significance

The Rigveda provides information about early Vedic society, particularly its northwestern geographical setting, rivers, cattle wealth, agriculture, kinship groups and political assemblies. Later Vedic literature reflects changes in agriculture, settlement, social organisation and ritual institutions.

These texts are valuable historical sources, but they are primarily religious compositions. Their descriptions must therefore be interpreted alongside archaeological and other evidence.

Prelims focus

  • The Rigveda is the oldest Veda and contains 10 Mandalas and 1028 Suktas in the Shakala recension.
  • The Samaveda is associated with melodic chanting; the Yajurveda with sacrificial formulas.
  • The Brahmanas explain rituals, while the Upanishads concentrate on philosophical enquiry.
  • Vyakarana, Nirukta and Chandas deal with grammar, etymology and poetic metre respectively.
  • Trap: The Vedangas are auxiliary disciplines, not additional Vedas.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 5, pp. 43–47, Chapter 7, pp. 65–74, and chronology on p. 134; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, pp. 84–86; IGNCA, Vedic Heritage Portal, Introduction and Rigveda Samhita and Samhitas sections, consulted 26 November 2026.]

body:
Itihasa: The Indian epic tradition

The Ramayana and Mahabharata are the 2 great Sanskrit epics of India. They belong to the literary tradition known as Itihasa. Both combine narratives about kings, families and conflicts with discussions of duty, morality, religion and political authority.

Neither epic was composed in its entire surviving form at a single moment. Stories were transmitted, expanded and reorganised over long periods. Regional languages subsequently developed their own versions of the narratives.

The Ramayana

The Sanskrit Ramayana is traditionally attributed to Valmiki, who is remembered as the Adi Kavi, or first poet, of the Sanskrit poetic tradition. The work is conventionally described as containing approximately 24,000 verses arranged in 7 Kandas, or books.

Its central narrative concerns Rama, Sita, Lakshmana and the conflict with Ravana. The story explores the relationship between personal duty, family obligations, kingship, loyalty and righteous conduct.

The Ramayana became a foundation for numerous regional literary traditions. Later authors did not merely translate it word for word; they adapted its language, religious emphasis and presentation to their own audiences.

The Mahabharata

The Mahabharata is traditionally attributed to Vyasa. Its principal narrative concerns the conflict between the Pandavas and Kauravas. In addition to the main story, the epic contains numerous legends, philosophical dialogues and discussions of governance and morality.

The work developed over approximately 1000 years beginning around 500 BCE. Its extensive surviving form contains about 100,000 verses, traditionally organised into 18 Parvas, or books.

The Bhagavad Gita forms part of the Bhishma Parva of the Mahabharata. It is a dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna that discusses duty, action, knowledge and devotion.

Important distinction

The Bhagavad Gita is part of the Mahabharata. The Upanishads belong to Vedic literature. Although these traditions share philosophical concepts, their literary classification is different.

The Puranas

Puranic literature developed through the preservation and expansion of religious narratives, legends, genealogies and accounts of creation. The tradition recognises 18 major Puranas, known as Mahapuranas, alongside numerous subsidiary works called Upapuranas.

Examples include the Vishnu Purana, Bhagavata Purana, Matsya Purana, Markandeya Purana and Shiva Purana. Their contents vary considerably, but important subjects include:

  • The creation and dissolution of the universe.
  • Genealogies of gods, sages and royal dynasties.
  • Accounts of sacred places and pilgrimage.
  • Devotion to particular deities and their incarnations.
  • Religious duties, customs and legends.

The Puranas helped communicate religious ideas to wider sections of society. Their stories could be heard through public recitation by people who did not have access to formal Vedic education.

Historians also use Puranic dynastic genealogies when reconstructing political history. Such genealogies must be compared with inscriptions, coins and other evidence because the texts contain mythology and were revised over time.

Dharma literature and social organisation

The Dharmasutras and Dharmashastras deal with religious duties, social conduct, inheritance, marriage, legal obligations and other aspects of normative life.

The Dharmasutras generally present rules in concise aphoristic prose. The Dharmashastras commonly present more extensive discussions in verse. An important example is the Manusmriti, also known as the Manava Dharmashastra, broadly dated between 200 BCE and 200 CE.

Such works help historians understand ideals concerning family organisation, varna, property and social obligations. However, a rule prescribed by a text does not establish that everyone followed it in practice.

Literature as historical evidence

Different literary forms reveal different aspects of the past. An epic may preserve social ideals and traditions of kingship, a Purana may preserve a royal genealogy, and a Dharma text may prescribe accepted conduct. Their historical value increases when their statements are compared with contemporary material evidence.

Prelims focus

  • Valmiki is traditionally associated with the Ramayana; Vyasa with the Mahabharata.
  • The Ramayana conventionally has 7 Kandas; the Mahabharata has 18 Parvas.
  • The Bhagavad Gita belongs to the Bhishma Parva.
  • The Puranic tradition recognises 18 Mahapuranas.
  • Manusmriti is a Dharmashastra concerned with normative duties and social conduct.
  • Trap: A prescription in a Dharma text is not proof of universal historical practice.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 12, pp. 127–130; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 3, pp. 53–65; Central Sanskrit University, About Sanskrit, sections on epic and Shastra literature, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: The Sanskrit Epics, Puranas and Dharma Literature

body:
Language and preservation of Buddhist teachings

Early Buddhism developed in a period when teachers increasingly communicated religious ideas through languages understood by ordinary people. Buddhist teachings were initially transmitted orally and were subsequently collected into organised textual traditions.

Pali, a Middle Indo-Aryan literary language, became particularly important in the Theravada Buddhist tradition. Buddhist authors also composed works in Sanskrit and other languages. Buddhist literature was therefore never restricted to a single language.

The Tripitaka

The principal canonical collection preserved in the Theravada tradition is the Tipitaka in Pali, also known by its Sanskrit name Tripitaka. The name means 3 baskets and refers to the division of Buddhist scriptures into 3 major collections.

  • Vinaya Pitaka: Rules governing the conduct and organisation of Buddhist monks and nuns. It is an important source for understanding the administration and discipline of the Sangha.
  • Sutta Pitaka: Discourses attributed principally to the Buddha and his disciples. It contains ethical teachings, dialogues, sermons and narrative compositions.
  • Abhidhamma Pitaka: Systematic analysis of Buddhist teachings, particularly concepts relating to consciousness, mental processes and existence.

Other Buddhist schools developed their own canonical arrangements. The Pali Tipitaka should therefore be understood specifically as the canon preserved by the Theravada tradition, rather than an identical collection accepted in every Buddhist school.

Important works within the Pali tradition

The Sutta Pitaka is divided into 5 collections known as Nikayas: Digha, Majjhima, Samyutta, Anguttara and Khuddaka. Several especially important literary works are associated with the Khuddaka Nikaya.

TextPrincipal subject
DhammapadaVerses concerning ethical conduct, wisdom and spiritual discipline
JatakaStories of previous births of the Buddha
TheragathaVerses associated with early Buddhist monks
TherigathaVerses associated with early Buddhist nuns
Sutta NipataEarly Buddhist discourses and poetic teachings

The Therigatha is especially valuable for understanding women's experiences of renunciation, spiritual freedom and religious life in ancient India.

Jataka stories communicate ethical lessons through narratives. They frequently describe merchants, artisans, rulers, travellers and ordinary households. Their influence extended beyond written literature to sculptures at Sanchi and paintings at Ajanta.

Other important Buddhist works

WorkAssociationImportance
MilindapanhaMenander and NagasenaDialogue on Buddhist philosophical questions
BuddhacharitaAshvaghoshaSanskrit poetic account of the Buddha's life
VisuddhimaggaBuddhaghosaSystematic exposition of Theravada doctrine and spiritual discipline
DipavamsaSri Lankan Buddhist traditionEarly Pali historical chronicle
MahavamsaTraditionally attributed to MahanamaPali chronicle of Sri Lanka and Buddhist history

Milindapanha presents a dialogue between the Indo-Greek ruler Menander, known as Milinda, and the Buddhist monk Nagasena. It illustrates the use of questions, analogies and reasoning to explain religious concepts.

Ashvaghosha, traditionally associated with the Kushana ruler Kanishka, composed Buddhacharita in Sanskrit. Buddhaghosa, associated with 5th-century CE Theravada scholarship in Sri Lanka, composed the Visuddhimagga in Pali.

Mahayana literature

The growth of Mahayana Buddhism produced an extensive literary tradition in Buddhist Sanskrit and related linguistic forms. Important examples include the Prajnaparamita texts, which discuss the perfection of wisdom, and the Saddharmapundarika Sutra, commonly called the Lotus Sutra.

The Lalitavistara presents an elaborate account of the Buddha's life. Buddhist Sanskrit works and their translations into Chinese and Tibetan helped transmit Buddhist ideas across Asia.

Historical significance

Buddhist literature provides evidence of urbanisation, trade, political institutions, religious debates, education and social relations. References to kingdoms and republics help reconstruct early political history, while monastic regulations reveal the organisation of religious communities.

Prelims focus

  • Vinaya concerns monastic discipline; Sutta concerns discourses; Abhidhamma concerns systematic doctrine.
  • The Therigatha preserves verses associated with Buddhist nuns.
  • Milindapanha is associated with Menander and Nagasena.
  • Ashvaghosha wrote Buddhacharita in Sanskrit.
  • Buddhaghosa is associated with the Pali Visuddhimagga.
  • Trap: Buddhist literature includes both Pali and Sanskrit works.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapters 7, 10 and 12, pp. 65–74, 100–106 and 129–130; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Themes 2 and 4, pp. 84–94 and 99–102; B. C. Law, A History of Pali Literature, sections on canonical and commentarial literature; Encyclopaedia of Buddhism, Milindapanha entry, consulted online 26 November 2026.]
